1	\begin{abstract}
2	Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models encode observations as hundreds of vision tokens, creating a computational bottleneck for real-time robotic control. Token pruning offers a training-free remedy, yet its effect varies dramatically across architectures: at retention ratio $k{=}0.95$, $\pi_{0.5}$ preserves 98\% task success while SmolVLA collapses to 0\%---why?
3	
4	We identify the vision-language connector as the primary architectural factor governing pruning tolerance. The coefficient of variation (CV) of post-connector token norms, computable in a single forward pass, predicts compressibility across the full architecture spectrum: from CV$\,{=}\,$0.038 (near-immune linear projection) to CV$\,{=}\,$0.314 (catastrophic pixel-shuffle collapse). Across six VLA architectures (450\,M--7\,B parameters) and four LIBERO manipulation suites, token-independent connectors degrade gracefully, while token-entangling connectors exhibit abrupt cliffs: SmolVLA collapses when just 6 of 128 tokens are removed.
5	
6	Importance-based selection is not universally beneficial---it can be actively harmful. L2 norm selection preserves 98\% success on $\pi_{0.5}$ where random yields 5\% (93\,pp gap); at aggressive ratios, random outperforms L2 by up to 36\,pp. No scoring method is universally safe: task complexity amplifies connector-dependent patterns (up to $20{\times}$ from Object to Goal at $k{=}0.9$). A zero-mask ablation isolates the mechanism: zeroing 10\% of tokens preserves 98.0\% SR while physical removal collapses to 9.0\%---the 89\,pp gap is entirely attributable to position disruption, not information loss. For architectures where all deletion fails, a lightweight re-encoding module (${\sim}$5\% extra parameters) recovers $>$60\% success at 75\% compression.
7	\end{abstract}

We present an empirical study of VLA token compressibility, identifying the vision-language connector as the primary determinant of pruning robustness (Figure~\ref{fig:teaser}). Token-independent connectors degrade gracefully; entangling connectors produce catastrophic failures amplified by task complexity (up to $20{\times}$ from Object to Goal at $k{=}0.9$). The coefficient of variation (CV) of post-connector token L2 norms captures this on a continuous spectrum (0.038 to 0.314). Under sufficient compression, scoring effectiveness becomes connector-dependent: L2 norm aids $\pi_{0.5}$ (up to $+$46.9\,pp on Long at $k{=}0.9$; $+$35.2\,pp on Goal at $k{=}0.85$) but reverses at aggressive ratios ($-$36\,pp at $k{=}0.5$); on X-VLA it is anti-informative ($-$8 to $-$27\,pp), while attention recovers near-baseline performance. For pixel-shuffle connectors where all pruning fails, Vision Token Re-encoder (VTR, ${\sim}$5\% extra parameters) recovers over 60\% SR at 75\% compression.

Our contributions are threefold: (1)~a compressibility analysis across six VLA architectures (450M--7B) on four LIBERO suites, identifying connector architecture as the primary determinant of pruning robustness; (2)~CV of token L2 norms as a single-pass diagnostic for connector compressibility type (uniform, graded, catastrophic), validated on four closed-loop architectures; and (3)~a zero-mask ablation proving position disruption---not information loss---drives $\pi_{0.5}$'s 89\,pp failure gap, plus VTR, which recovers a pixel-shuffle VLA from 0\% to over 60\% at 75\% compression.
tool_args.new_string:
We present an empirical study of VLA token compressibility across six architectures (450M--7B) and four LIBERO manipulation suites, identifying the vision-language connector as the primary determinant of pruning robustness (Figure~\ref{fig:teaser}). Three findings emerge:

\emph{First, connector architecture governs the degradation pattern.} Token-independent connectors (linear projections, MLPs) degrade gracefully under pruning, while token-entangling connectors (BART encoders, pixel-shuffle) produce catastrophic cliffs---and task complexity amplifies the gap by up to $20{\times}$.

\emph{Second, no scoring method is universally safe.} L2 norm selection can dramatically outperform random pruning on one architecture yet \emph{reverse} on another; the advantage follows an inverted-U curve that peaks at moderate compression and collapses at aggressive ratios. Which method helps---or harms---depends on the connector's token information structure.

\emph{Third, a zero-cost diagnostic predicts these behaviors.} The coefficient of variation (CV) of post-connector token L2 norms, computable from a single forward pass, partitions architectures into compressibility regimes and predicts both pruning tolerance and the threshold at which scoring method choice becomes critical. For architectures where all deletion fails, a lightweight Vision Token Re-encoder (VTR, ${\sim}$5\% extra parameters) recovers over 60\% success rate at 75\% compression.

Our contributions are: (1)~the first cross-architecture compressibility analysis of VLA token pruning, revealing connector type as the dominant factor; (2)~CV as a single-pass diagnostic that predicts pruning tolerance and scoring method sensitivity; and (3)~mechanistic evidence that position disruption---not information loss---drives pruning failure in low-CV architectures, plus VTR as a recovery path for entangling connectors.

Given $N$ post-connector tokens $\{t_1, \ldots, t_N\}$ with $t_i \in \mathbb{R}^d$, token pruning retains $\lfloor k \cdot N \rfloor$ tokens for $k \in (0, 1]$ and physically removes the rest, re-indexing positions to close gaps. We prune between the connector output and LLM input to isolate the connector's effect on token information structure.

\paragraph{Importance scoring functions.}
A scoring function $s\colon \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}$ assigns each token an importance score; the top-$\lfloor kN \rfloor$ tokens by score are retained. We evaluate two backbone-agnostic strategies.

\textbf{L2-norm scoring} uses activation magnitude $s_{\text{L2}}(t_i) = \|t_i\|_2$ as a proxy for information density. L2 scoring introduces spatial bias: nearby patches produce correlated norms, so aggressive pruning can concentrate retained tokens in a single region (Section~\ref{sec:cv_sensitivity}).

\textbf{Random subsampling} draws $\lfloor kN \rfloor$ tokens uniformly ($s_{\text{rand}}(t_i) \sim \mathcal{U}(0, 1)$), providing a null hypothesis that all tokens are interchangeable. Random selection preserves spatial coverage in expectation, making it the natural baseline for spatially uniform architectures. Sampling variance is controlled through multi-seed evaluation (Section~\ref{sec:exp_setup}).

The \emph{importance margin} $\Delta(k) = \text{SR}_{\text{L2}}(k) - \text{SR}_{\text{Random}}(k)$ quantifies exploitable importance structure. A negative margin indicates L2 selection is actively harmful. The sign and magnitude of $\Delta$ vary systematically with connector CV and $k$ (Section~\ref{sec:cv_sensitivity}). We also evaluate attention-based scoring on selected conditions (Appendix~\ref{app:attention_scoring}); we focus on L2 and random because they operate solely on the connector output and suffice to reveal connector-dependent importance structure.

\paragraph{Retention ratios.}
We evaluate $k \in \{0.30, 0.50, 0.70, 0.75, 0.85, 0.90, 0.95\}$, spanning extreme compression to conservative trimming. This range identifies \emph{cliff zones}: narrow $k$ intervals where SR drops discontinuously. Different connectors cliff at different ratios: pixel-shuffle at $k{=}0.95$, BART-encoded near $k{\approx}0.85$, MLP without a sharp cliff (Appendix~\ref{app:pruning_details}).

Given $N$ post-connector tokens $\{t_1, \ldots, t_N\}$ with $t_i \in \mathbb{R}^d$, token pruning retains $\lfloor k \cdot N \rfloor$ tokens for $k \in (0, 1]$ and physically removes the rest. Crucially, we \emph{re-index} the remaining positions contiguously (i.e., the $j$-th retained token receives position ID $j$) rather than preserving original position IDs. This choice isolates two confounded effects: information loss from removing tokens and position disruption from re-indexing. We prune between the connector output and LLM input to isolate the connector's effect on token information structure; the vision encoder and LLM weights remain frozen throughout.

\paragraph{Importance scoring functions.}
A scoring function $s\colon \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}$ assigns each token an importance score; the top-$\lfloor kN \rfloor$ tokens by score are retained. We evaluate two backbone-agnostic strategies that require only the connector output, not LLM internals.

\textbf{L2-norm scoring} uses activation magnitude $s_{\text{L2}}(t_i) = \|t_i\|_2$ as a proxy for information density. For each image, we compute the L2 norm of every post-connector token, rank tokens in descending order, and retain the top-$\lfloor kN \rfloor$. L2 scoring introduces spatial bias: nearby patches share similar visual content and produce correlated norms, so aggressive pruning can concentrate retained tokens in a single spatial region at the expense of scene coverage (Section~\ref{sec:cv_sensitivity}).

\textbf{Random subsampling} draws $\lfloor kN \rfloor$ tokens uniformly without replacement ($s_{\text{rand}}(t_i) \sim \mathcal{U}(0, 1)$), providing a null hypothesis that all tokens are interchangeable. Random selection preserves spatial coverage in expectation, making it the natural baseline for spatially uniform architectures. To control sampling variance, we report results over multiple seeds (Section~\ref{sec:exp_setup}).

We also evaluate \textbf{attention-based scoring} on selected conditions: for each vision token, we sum the attention weights it receives from all action-query tokens across all LLM layers, yielding an importance score that reflects the LLM's actual usage pattern. Results appear in Appendix~\ref{app:attention_scoring}; we focus on L2 and random in the main text because they operate solely on the connector output and suffice to reveal connector-dependent importance structure.

The \emph{importance margin} $\Delta(k) = \text{SR}_{\text{L2}}(k) - \text{SR}_{\text{Random}}(k)$ quantifies exploitable importance structure at each retention ratio. A positive margin means the token importance landscape is informative---L2 norm successfully identifies dispensable tokens. A negative margin indicates L2 selection is actively harmful, clustering spatially correlated tokens while discarding critical spatial coverage. The sign and magnitude of $\Delta$ vary systematically with connector CV and $k$ (Section~\ref{sec:cv_sensitivity}).

\paragraph{Retention ratios and evaluation.}
We evaluate $k \in \{0.30, 0.50, 0.70, 0.75, 0.85, 0.90, 0.95\}$, spanning extreme compression to conservative trimming. For each model--suite--method--$k$ combination, we run all 50 evaluation episodes per task (10 tasks $\times$ 50 episodes $=$ 500 total) and report mean success rate (SR). Multi-seed conditions ($\pi_{0.5}$ Long: $n{=}5$ seeds; VTR: $n{=}3$) report mean $\pm$ sample standard deviation. This range identifies \emph{cliff zones}: narrow $k$ intervals where SR drops discontinuously. Different connectors cliff at different ratios: pixel-shuffle at $k{=}0.95$, BART-encoded near $k{\approx}0.85$, MLP without a sharp cliff (Appendix~\ref{app:pruning_details}).
